scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tobas originated in Oruro, Bolivia, in the early 20th century when Tomás Cáceres Nava and his son Donato, inspired by the Chunchos dance seen at the San Roque festival in Tarija, created a comparsa around 1905.
The dance was named after the Toba tribe, feared warriors from the Chaco region, popularized by the mysterious death of explorer Jules Crevaux in 1882.
on_screen: Map: Bolivia · South America

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Tobas is performed at major Bolivian festivals including Carnaval de Oruro and Fiesta del Gran Poder, and internationally in festivals in Chile, Peru, and Argentina.
The dance conveys messages of indigenous identity preservation, respect for nature and biodiversity, and cultural diversity awareness.
It transmits ancestral and historical cultural legacy to future generations.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Originally, Tobas music used traditional Andean wind instruments like pinquillos and quenas.
From the 1960s onward, brass instruments replaced these, creating a more agile and energetic sound.
Listen for the pinquillos, quenas, brass instruments.
The music transitioned from traditional Andean wind instruments to brass, creating a lively and agile sound that supports the vigorous jumps and rapid footwork of the dance.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear elaborate costumes featuring full feathered headdresses decorated with jewels, colorful skirts and tops adorned with beads and fringes, and anklets with sewn cow hooves that add rhythmic sounds.
They carry symbolic weapons such as spears or hatchets and wear feather bracelets.
The dance is performed outdoors during religious and cultural festivals like Carnaval de Oruro and Fiesta del Gran Poder, as well as international events in Chile, Peru, and Argentina.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Tomás Cáceres Nava and his son Donato Cáceres Véliz founded the original comparsa inspired by the Chunchos dance.
Cristóbal Franco founded the Comparsa Tobas Zona Central in 1945, promoting native dances for decades.
The dance is performed mainly in Oruro but also appears in festivals in other Bolivian regions such as Beni and La Paz, where the costume reflects Amazonian influences.
Tobas is a Bolivian folk dance inspired by the Chunchos dance of Tarija and named after the Toba tribe of the Chaco region.
